From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Subject: Post-call recap: tool/function-calls + structured outputs — recap & proposed next steps

Hi James (and team),

Thanks again for a productive 30-minute call today — appreciate you walking us through the ingestion pipeline and the function-calling scenario you’re trying to stabilize. Below is a short recap, the criteria you emphasized, and proposed next steps. Please reply with any corrections or additions.

Quick recap (what we heard)
- Pain: downstream services (transactions & reconciliation) rely on strictly-formatted JSON from the model; malformed outputs create manual reconciliation work.
- Current stack: internal extraction service -> post-processing microservice (Python) -> rules engine (Java). Model outputs currently run through a brittle set of regex rules.
- Goal: deterministically formatted function-call style outputs (JSON schema validated) so you can auto-ingest without manual fixes.
- SLOs you mentioned: >95% schema-conformant outputs on production prompts, end-to-end median latency target <250ms, and integration with your existing event bus (Kafka).

Success criteria (as discussed)
1) Deterministic formatting: schema enforcement or function-calling contract such that outputs validate against your ingestion schema.
2) Low tail latency: keep 99th percentile under 500ms for standard 512-token prompts (we discussed batching trade-offs).
3) Observability: token-level breakdown + per-route error rates so your SREs can triage regressions quickly.

Specific ask re: function-calling + structured outputs
- You need the model to emit a single JSON object that adheres to your existing reconciliation schema (attached: example-json-schema.json).
- We discussed two enforcement options: 1) model-side function call semantics (strict name/args contract) + post-validate, or 2) Redwood’s schema-enforcement layer that rejects/repairs non-conformant outputs before they hit the stream.

Proposed next steps
1) You: share a small set (50–100) of representative prompts + expected JSON objects we can use for evaluation (due: Apr 10).
2) Redwood: run a focused eval (schema-conformance + latency) and share a short report (target by Apr 17).
3) Technical deep-dive: schedule a 60-minute session with your API/infra folks and our SE (Marissa) week of Apr 20 to review an architecture diagram and POC plan.
4) Optional: short POC (3–4 weeks) to demonstrate automated JSON outputs and integration with your staging Kafka topic.

Attachments: discovery-notes-vanessa-20260403.pdf (call notes), example-json-schema.json (your target schema example).

If that all looks right, I’ll queue the eval and propose 2 time slots for the deep-dive.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz
Senior AE, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: tool/function-calls + structured outputs — recap & proposed next steps

James — great, thanks for the quick reply and the timeline note. To answer your questions:

1) Schema-enforcement flow (short description)
- Redwood can operate in two modes for this use case:
  a) Validation+Reject: the runtime validates the model's JSON against your schema and rejects responses that fail; those requests can be retried (with different decoding parameters) or routed to a fallback model.
  b) Validation+Auto-repair: an intermediate agent attempts a deterministic repair using a constrained function call to a small repair policy (e.g., cast types, fill missing keys with null/defaults) — only applied when the repair passes a final validation step.

Both approaches are compatible with your ingestion path; for the POC we usually recommend Validation+Auto-repair so you can measure both raw model conformance and the repaired pass-rate.

2) Who will run the eval- Marissa Cole (SE) and Aditya Rao (Solutions Architect) will run the initial eval and present results. Marissa will lead the deep-dive.

Inline example: minimal function-calling contract + JSON schema snippet (we attached the full example-json-schema.json but included a tiny example inline):

-- start schema snippet --
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "transaction_id": {"type": "string"},
    "amount_cents": {"type": "integer"},
    "currency": {"type": "string"},
    "timestamp": {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}
  },
  "required": ["transaction_id","amount_cents","currency","timestamp"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
-- end schema snippet --

Agent/workflow mapping (high level)
- Ingest prompt -> Redwood runtime (function-call enforced) -> Validation layer -> Repair agent (optional) -> Post-processing microservice -> Kafka topic.
- Observability hooks: return an enforcement flag on the token-level cost trace and a per-request validation result tag so you can track which items were repaired vs. accepted.

Proposed next steps (updated)
- You: share 50 prompts + expected outputs by Apr 9.
- Redwood: run conformance + latency eval and deliver a short report by Apr 17.
- Deep-dive: Marissa proposes Apr 21, 9:30am PT or Apr 22, 11:00am PT — are either of those good for your infra team?
- POC pricing: we’ll send an indicative 3-week POC price sheet before the deep-dive (Marissa).

Attachments: redwood-poc-plan-2026-04-03.xlsx (POC timeline & roles).

If that schedule works I’ll book the deep-dive and start the eval run.

Thanks,
Vanessa
